extracted.intended_audience: scientists, surveyors, anthropologists, and educated public interested in 19th-century U.S. survey/ethnographic practice and policy
extracted.subtask_description: Historical discussion of the organization, consolidation, and scientific standards for U.S. government surveys (geological, topographical, ethnographic) and related practises for collecting and publishing ethnological and archaeological materials. Covers recommendations about departmental control, division of labor, data custody, and methods of scientific work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of overlapping surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of multiple, independent surveys operating in the same and contiguous areas should be unified under a single management or common system to avoid duplication and discordant methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professor Powell argued that if both departments survey the entire region there will be duplicated atlases and twice the work; consolidation may be accomplished by act of Congress, executive direction, or placing the work under one management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor by branch of natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: Each branch of natural history should be prosecuted wholly by a single division which is in possession of all the materials for that branch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powell proposed that divisions specialize (e.g., ethnography, geology) and either turn over or receive materials collected by other surveys to avoid duplication and ensure coherent treatment of each discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental allocation of survey responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys necessary for military purposes should be continued under the War Department; all other surveys for geographical, geological, topographical, and scientific purposes should be continued under the Department of the Interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the committee recommendation after competing claims by War and Interior departments; differentiates mapping for military operations from broader scientific mapping and resource study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effective, standardized mapping system
rubrics_metrics.description: A plan for surveying and mapping the Territories should follow a general system that secures the best results at the least possible cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congressional provision required the National Academy of Sciences to consider such a plan; emphasis is on general systematization and economy in national mapping efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent organization and presidential appointment of director
rubrics_metrics.description: The geological survey should be established as an independent organization under the Department of the Interior, with its director appointed by the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The National Academy's report recommended formation of the United States Geological Survey on this governance model; implies expectation of national-level leadership and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized custody and publication of ethnological materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials collected by surveys bearing on ethnology should be turned over to the Smithsonian Institution (Bureau of Ethnology) for completion, preparation, and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appropriation provided for completing the 'Contributions to North American Ethnology' under the Smithsonian with a provision that relevant survey materials be deposited there; this established a central repository/center for ethnographic operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urgency of language documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Study and collection of Indian languages must be undertaken promptly because languages are already becoming corrupted and may soon be impossible to study scientifically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powell emphasized that even if indigenous peoples survive, their languages were deteriorating, creating a time-sensitive imperative for linguistic documentation and collection during surveys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific (realistic, objective) approach in anthropology
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropology should belong to the strictly scientific school that rejects imaginative and poetical accounts of lower races and approaches phenomena from an objective point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powell is described as belonging to the school represented by Lewis H. Morgan; he accepts evolution but also critiques inadequacies in some systematic developments — stressing rigorous, empirical methods over romanticized narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation must be combined with theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Good scientific practice requires both careful observation and deep thinking; observation without theory is sterile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powell's stated principle that to observe well one must also think deeply and that he applies this idea practically when selecting assistants; implies hiring and analytic standards for scientific teams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for selecting scientific assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: Assistants should be chosen for their capacity to observe and think deeply, preference for persons of culture and independence of thought; selection should avoid offense to others while securing these qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powell's personnel selection is described as guided by these intellectual and character traits, reflecting standards for research team composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for property rights and controlled data sharing in fieldwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers/owners of sites (e.g., Mammoth Cave trustees) may modify or suppress maps while still encouraging scientific investigation; scientists should respect reasonable restrictions while using instruments and sharing results appropriate for scientific ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter notes manager Klett allowed use of barometers and pedometers and let the author present results to the American Association but requested certain scale/details not be published; editor's note acknowledges reliance on imperfect newspaper reports—this describes a balance between proprietary control and scientific transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/practical technique for entomological specimen preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid prolonged suffering of insects during pinning, entomologists should dip pins in prussic acid so the effect is instantaneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed as a means to end dispute about insect pain—practical guidance for specimen collection to minimize suffering and preserve specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication and expert evaluation of anomalous archaeological finds
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscribed or otherwise extraordinary archaeological objects found within the United States should be subjected to expert opinion and scrutiny to establish genuineness or to convict frauds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author solicits assessments from named authorities (museum and Smithsonian experts, anthropological section leaders), urging specialists to lend their aid in verifying or refuting the authenticity of items like the Piqua tablets and Davenport slates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in secondary reportage of scientific proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: When summarizing papers or proceedings, one should not rely excessively on daily newspaper reports because they are often imperfect and can misrepresent the author's meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor's note adds this correction after a correspondent's letter about an earlier report — an editorial standard for accurate reporting of scientific meetings.
